passage: At school break, Yash had the class bat and five friends all shouting, 'Me first!' He stood by the wall, thinking. It was like the library. Usha Ma'am had solved that last month by letting children borrow books in roll-number order. 'Same thing,' Yash muttered. He tore a page from his rough notebook, wrote the five names in a column, and numbered them one to five. 'After your turn, you go to the bottom,' he told them. 'Tomorrow we start with whoever is next.' Urmila complained for a moment that she was fifth, then nodded. When the bell rang, Yash pinned the list on the wall under the clock.

What did Yash think when he remembered the library?
qa.a: Yash thought it was the same kind of problem, so the same kind of answer could work, and he felt confident.

qa.q: What could Yash do if a friend was away on the next day?
qa.a: Yash could skip that friend for the day and keep their place at the top, so nobody loses a turn because of being absent.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt about being fifth?
qa.a: Urmila was probably annoyed for a moment, then accepted it once she saw that everyone waits in the same order.

I'm Ramesh, and I live in the same colony as Darshan. Every evening there was a fight about cricket turns. Five of them, one bat. Whoever shouted loudest batted first, and little Joseph never got a turn.
Last Monday Darshan came down with a sheet of paper. He said, "Remember in school, the library went by roll numbers, so nobody fought? Let's do the same."
He wrote all five names in a list. Batting order, one to five. Next day, whoever batted first moves to the bottom and everyone moves up one.
That evening there was no shouting. On Wednesday Joseph was first, and he hit a four off the first ball.
I don't know what Darshan was feeling when Joseph hit it. But he was clapping hardest.

qa.q: How many friends shared the one bat?
qa.a: Five of them shared one bat.

qa.q: What might Darshan's clapping hardest suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Darshan felt happy and proud that his fair list gave Joseph a real turn, though the observer can't be sure.

qa.q: Which other way of sharing turns could work, and why might the list still be better?
qa.a: They could toss a coin each day, but the rotating list is better because everyone can see when their turn is coming.

qa.q: How is Joseph affected by the new list?
qa.a: Joseph finally gets to bat first on Wednesday, after never getting a turn, and hits a four off the first ball.

Friday. The building's cricket gang broke up in tears again. Farhan's little cousin Trisha said the big boys always batted first and she only fielded. Farhan, who was ten, went home cross.
Saturday. Lying on his bed, he remembered class. When everyone fought over library books, Ma'am had made a list by roll number, and each week the first person went to the end. Nobody fought after that.
He took his school diary and wrote five names. Trisha first, because she had waited longest.
Monday. At the park, he read the list aloud and pinned it to the gate with a clothes clip. "Tomorrow, Trisha goes to the end, and I move up." The older boys grumbled, then shrugged.
Trisha got to bat for ten whole overs. She waved her bat at Farhan like a champion.

qa.q: Where did Farhan pin the list?
qa.a: He pinned it to the gate with a clothes clip.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he went home on Friday?
qa.a: He was cross and upset that the game had broken up in tears again and Trisha only got to field.

qa.q: What else could Farhan add to make the list feel fair to the older boys?
qa.a: He could let everyone agree on the starting order, so the older boys feel included and don't just grumble.

qa.q: How does Trisha experience the new list?
qa.a: Trisha finally gets to bat for ten whole overs and feels like a champion, waving her bat at Farhan.
